prompt: Why does `watch(minutes.value, …)` not do what its author meant?
hint: What is `minutes.value` at the moment the line runs?

choices.text: It watches `minutes` deeply, which is slower
choices.why: Depth is not the problem: nothing reactive was passed at all.

choices.text: It passes the number 30, which Vue cannot track
choices.why: Right. Pass the ref itself; Vue warns about a source like this one.

choices.text: It fires on every render instead of on every change
choices.why: It never fires. What it received is a value, not a source.

choices.text: It works, without the old value
choices.why: The old value comes with any source that works; this one does not work.

prompt: In `WatchSources`, the watcher on the getter `() => minutes.value >= 60` printed once, at 60. Why did it stay silent at 45?
hint: What did the getter return before that change, and after it?

choices.text: A getter skips the first change it sees
choices.why: There is no such rule; the getter is run again on every change of what it read.

choices.text: The array watcher took that change first
choices.why: Each watcher is independent; one firing takes nothing away from the others.

choices.text: Its result was `false` before and after
choices.why: Right. 30 and 45 both give `false`, and the callback runs when the result changes; 60 is the first `true`.

choices.text: Vue tracked `minutes` from 60 on, when the getter first returned something
choices.why: It tracked `minutes` from the first run; the getter ran at 45 too, and returned `false` again.

prompt: In the `WatchSources` transcript, how many of the three watchers fired on the click on `Guitar`?
hint: Count the lines under `-- click #guitar`.

prompt: In `DeepAndOnce`, which watchers fired on the first click on `Push a session`? Choose all that apply.
hint: A push changes the array that is already in `.value`.

choices.text: The one with `deep: true`
choices.why: Right. A push changes something inside, and a deep watcher reads everything inside.

choices.text: The plain watcher on the ref
choices.why: Nothing was replaced, so a shallow watcher saw nothing; it missed both pushes.

choices.text: The one on the `reactive` object
choices.why: Right. A `reactive` object is watched deeply without asking.

choices.text: The one with `immediate: true`
choices.why: It ran when the page opened and then behaves like a plain watcher, which a push does not wake.

choices.text: The one with `once: true` and deep
choices.why: Right. It is deep, and this was its first change; it did not run again.

prompt: The watcher on the `reactive` object `plan` fired on both pushes and not on `Replace the list`. Why not on the replace?
hint: Look at what `replace()` assigns to.

choices.text: A `reactive` object is watched shallowly
choices.why: The opposite: it is watched deeply without asking, which is why it saw the pushes.

choices.text: Copying an array with `[...]` is not a reactive change at all
choices.why: The ref's own watchers fired on the replace, so it was a change; just not to `plan`.

choices.text: It had already used up its one run
choices.why: That is the `once` watcher; this one has no `once`.

choices.text: `replace` gave the ref `sessions` a new array and left `plan` alone
choices.why: Right. The two buttons change different things, and only `push` touched `plan`.

prompt: A list of ten thousand sessions is watched with `deep: true` only to show how many there are. What does the lesson's advice point to?
hint: What is the one thing this watcher needs?

choices.text: Adding `immediate: true`, so that the walk happens once
choices.why: `immediate` adds a run at the start; every later change is still a walk of the whole tree.

choices.text: A getter: `() => sessions.value.length`
choices.why: Right. It fires when the count changes and reads nothing else.

choices.text: `flush: 'sync'`, to keep the cost down
choices.why: `'sync'` runs it on every single write, which costs more, not less.

choices.text: Moving the list into `reactive` instead of a ref
choices.why: A `reactive` object is watched deeply anyway: the same walk, without the option written.

prompt: In `EffectTracking`, the async effect reads `note`, and yet `Add a note` re-ran nothing. Why?
hint: Where in the function is `note` read?

choices.text: `note` starts as an empty string, which is not reactive
choices.why: An empty string in a ref is as reactive as any other value.

choices.text: An async effect runs once, when the page opens, and stops
choices.why: It re-ran on `Spanish`, because it had read `course` before the `await`.

choices.text: The first effect had claimed `note`
choices.why: Effects do not share or claim sources, and the first one never read `note`.

choices.text: It is read after the `await`, when Vue had stopped recording
choices.why: Right. Tracking lasts while the function runs synchronously; the reads after it count for nothing.

prompt: In an async `watchEffect`, read every source you depend on before the first ___, into local constants.
hint: The keyword where the function pauses.

prompt: Why does a `watchEffect` run once as soon as it is created?
hint: It has no source argument.

choices.text: It is a `watch` with `immediate: true`, written shorter
choices.why: It differs more than that: it has no named sources and no old value.

choices.text: Vue runs every watcher once when a component is set up
choices.why: A `watch` does not run until the first change, unless `immediate` is set.

choices.text: Running it is how it finds its sources
choices.why: Right. Its first run records what it reads, and that is what it then watches.

choices.text: To store the old values before any change arrives
choices.why: A `watchEffect` gives you no old value; the table in this section says so.

prompt: One click on `Add two` in `FlushTiming`. How many times did the `'sync'` watcher run?
hint: Count the lines that start with `sync:`.

prompt: A watcher scrolls a list to the session that was just added. Which `flush` does it need?
hint: Does the new session's element exist yet?

choices.text: `'pre'`, since it is the default
choices.why: Before the redraw, the new session's element does not exist yet.

choices.text: `'sync'`, so that it runs at the moment of the write
choices.why: At the moment of the write the page still shows the old list, as `page says 0` did.

choices.text: Any of the three, because the value is the same in all of them
choices.why: The value is the same; the page is not, and scrolling needs the page.

choices.text: `'post'`
choices.why: Right. The element exists only after the redraw.

prompt: The default watcher printed `pre:  count 2, page says 0`. What does that line show?
hint: Compare it with the `sync` lines and the `post` line around it.

choices.text: It ran at the first write and missed the second
choices.why: Then it would have said count 1, as the first `sync` line did.

choices.text: Once, with the final value, before the redraw
choices.why: Right. Both writes were batched, and the page had not been redrawn yet.

choices.text: The redraw failed and the page stayed at 0
choices.why: The `post` line, a moment later, saw the page say 2.

choices.text: It read the page before Vue had even started its queue for that click
choices.why: It runs from the queue; its place in the queue is before the redraw.

prompt: Why does the careless watcher end up showing the notes for statistics, while the course chosen is Spanish?
hint: Look at when each answer arrived.

choices.text: Statistics was asked first, so Vue shows its answer
choices.why: Vue does not order the answers; the last assignment wins.

choices.text: The slow answer landed last and overwrote the fast one
choices.why: Right. Both requests were in flight; statistics answered 500 milliseconds after Spanish.

choices.text: Spanish's request failed without saying so
choices.why: Nothing failed: Spanish answered after 100 milliseconds and was shown.

choices.text: The watcher fired for the first change and not the second
choices.why: It fired for both; that is why two requests were in flight.

prompt: When does Vue call a function registered with `onWatcherCleanup`?
hint: In the demo, the statistics run's flag was set when Spanish was chosen.

choices.text: When the `await` inside the callback resolves
choices.why: The answer arriving calls nothing; the next change does.

choices.text: After the component redraws
choices.why: That is `flush: 'post'`, which is about the callback, not the cleanup.

choices.text: Just before the watcher runs again, and when it is stopped
choices.why: Right. So the statistics run was marked stale before the Spanish run began.

choices.text: Once, when the component is removed from the page
choices.why: Removal stops the watcher and calls it then, but it is also called before every new run.

prompt: About cancelling a stale request, which of these does the section support? Choose all that apply.
hint: A flag ignores; an `AbortController` stops.

choices.text: With a `stale` flag, the slow request still runs to the end
choices.why: Right. The flag only decides that its answer is thrown away.

choices.text: A cleanup registered after the first `await` is tied to its run as well
choices.why: Registered after an `await`, Vue cannot tell which run it belongs to, and warns.

choices.text: `controller.abort()` makes the pending `fetch` reject with an `AbortError`
choices.why: Right. So the lines after the `fetch` never run for the stale course.

choices.text: Aborting also needs the `stale` flag, or the old answer still lands
choices.why: An aborted `fetch` rejects, so the assignment after it never happens.

prompt: Since Vue 3.5, `___(fn)`, called inside a watcher's callback, registers a function that belongs to that run.
hint: `StaleAnswer` imports it from `vue`.

prompt: After `Remove the listener`, the late watcher alone saw tick 3. Why that one?
hint: Look at when each of the three was created.

choices.text: It was the last to be registered, so Vue keeps it
choices.why: Vue keeps nothing by order; what matters is whether a component was being set up.

choices.text: It watches `tick` through the module rather than the component
choices.why: All three watch the same `tick` from the same module.

choices.text: The setup watcher had called `stop()` on the first tick
choices.why: That was the stoppable watcher; the setup watcher saw tick 2 and then stopped with the component.

choices.text: It was created in a `setTimeout`, after setup
choices.why: Right. No component was being set up then, so it belongs to nobody and removing the component does not stop it.

prompt: In a `<script setup>`, a watcher is created on the line after `await loadCourses()`. The component is shown and hidden many times. What follows from the lesson?
hint: What does Vue know about the component once the `await` has resumed?

choices.text: The watchers pile up: keep each stop function and call it in `onUnmounted`
choices.why: Right. Created after an `await`, it belongs to nobody and outlives its component.

choices.text: Nothing changes: the line is still at the top level of the script
choices.why: It is written at the top level but runs after the `await`, when no component is being set up.

choices.text: Vue stops it at the next change of its source
choices.why: A change runs it; nothing stops a watcher that belongs to nobody until the page closes.

choices.text: It runs once and stops, as with `{ once: true }`
choices.why: `once` is an option you pass; an `await` does not add it.

prompt: What do `watch` and `watchEffect` return?
hint: The stoppable watcher in `Listener` keeps it in a constant.

choices.text: The watcher's first result
choices.why: For a `watch`, nothing has run yet when it returns.

choices.text: A promise that resolves on the first change
choices.why: There is no promise; the demo calls what was returned directly, as a function.

choices.text: A ref that holds the latest value
choices.why: That is closer to a `computed`; a watcher's return value is how you stop it.

choices.text: A function that stops the watcher
choices.why: Right. In Vue 3.5 the same handle also has `pause()` and `resume()`.

prompt: Why is a shallow watcher on `sessions` enough to keep the browser's copy current?
hint: How do the planner's rules change the list?

choices.text: `localStorage` keeps its own copy in step with the ref
choices.why: `localStorage` keeps what it was last given; nothing in it follows the ref.

choices.text: The rules return new arrays, so every change is a new `.value`
choices.why: Right. `toggleDone` and `addSession` never change the list they are given.

choices.text: `JSON.stringify` reads the whole list, which makes the watcher deep
choices.why: It reads the list when the callback runs; it has no say in when the callback runs.

choices.text: The planner never changes its sessions
choices.why: Not yet; lessons 5 and 14 do, and they replace the list each time.

prompt: `courses.json` gains a new session. A student whose browser has a saved copy reloads the page. What does the planner show?
hint: Read the line that assigns `sessions.value`.

choices.text: The file's list, because the file is the source
choices.why: The sessions come from the browser's copy when there is one; the courses alone come from the file.

choices.text: Both lists, merged
choices.why: Nothing merges them; `saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : data.sessions` picks one of the two.

choices.text: An error saying that the courses could not be loaded
choices.why: That is what a copy that is not valid JSON would cause, not a changed file.

choices.text: The saved copy, without the new session
choices.why: Right. The copy wins, and the lesson calls that the right answer for sessions that belong to the student.

prompt: Why does the capture of the planner add `--do 'goto /'`?
hint: What does `look` have stored when it starts?

choices.text: `look` starts with an empty browser every time
choices.why: Right. So the page is loaded twice in one browser, and the second load finds the copy the first one saved.

choices.text: To wait for the watcher to finish saving
choices.why: The watcher saves as soon as the list is assigned; the second load is about reading the copy back.

choices.text: To clear `localStorage` before the run
choices.why: It does the opposite: it keeps the same browser, with what was stored.

choices.text: The first load reads the copy and the second one the file
choices.why: The other way round: the first visit read the file, the second the copy.

prompt: Put what happens around `StaleAnswer`'s careful watcher in order, from the click on `Statistics` to the end of the wait.
hint: The cleanup runs before the next run starts, not when an answer arrives.
items: The course becomes statistics, and its run asks the slow server
Vue calls the statistics run's cleanup, which sets its `stale`
The Spanish run asks, and its answer is shown after 100 milliseconds
The statistics answer arrives, and its run drops it

prompt: Match each option to what it changes about a watcher.
hint: One description on the right belongs to an option that is not on the left.

pairs.right: notices a change anywhere inside the value

right_distractors: runs at the moment of every write

prompt: `watchEffect(async () => { await loadSettings(); notes.value = await lookUp(course.value) })`. The student picks another course. What happens?
hint: Where is `course` read, relative to the first `await`?

choices.text: The effect runs again and fetches the new course's notes
choices.why: That needs `course` read before the first `await`; here it is read after it.

choices.text: It runs again twice, once for each `await`
choices.why: `await`s do not make runs; changes to tracked sources do, and this effect tracked none.

choices.text: Vue warns that `course` was read too late, and runs it again anyway
choices.why: There is no warning; that silence is the trap the lesson names.

choices.text: Nothing: `course` was read after an `await`, so it is not a source
choices.why: Right. The notes stay those of the first course, and nothing says so.
